critique.good: All four columns fit in the viewport, so readers can see the page and its audit result together without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Rows become extremely tall and hard to scan. Titles and URLs fracture within words, dates split across lines, and the URL column dominates the table vertically while the result columns contain large empty areas.
critique.cause: The 100px title and 109px URL columns leave only 79px and 88px for text. The 82px date column also leaves too little room for a complete date.

critique.good: The wider title and URL columns make rows substantially shorter and keep most title words intact. The title and most of each URL are visible initially.
critique.problems: Some URL segments still split awkwardly, and dates remain broken across lines. The viewport cuts into the date column and hides the status column, making the audit results hard to discover and compare with their pages.
critique.cause: The 210px URL width still forces splits in long segments. The 82px date width is insufficient for a complete date, while the first two columns consume 355px before the result columns begin.

critique.good: Titles and URLs read more naturally, dates and status codes remain intact, and the unwrapped headers establish a clear hierarchy. The shorter rows make comparisons easier once the relevant columns are in view.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows the title and only part of the URL; both audit-result columns are far offscreen. Readers must scroll a long way and maintain their place across rows to connect a page with its result.
critique.cause: The 180px title and 345px URL columns put the result columns 525px from the table's left edge. The generous 117px and 107px result columns add further horizontal travel.

critique.good: The title column gives most page names a readable shape, and the URL column keeps rows substantially shorter than in r1C. The row borders help readers follow each record.
critique.problems: Several URL segments split within words, while the audit results sit entirely beyond the initial viewport. The narrow date column also risks splitting dates, weakening comparison.
critique.cause: The 230px URL column leaves 209px for text; the 105px date column leaves 84px, less than the 96px needed for its longest one-line content.

critique.good: This is the strongest overall balance: titles wrap naturally, URLs have fewer mid-word splits, and the shorter rows make the inventory easier to scan.
critique.problems: The first viewport shows titles and only part of each URL; both audit columns require horizontal scrolling. Some URL segments still split, and dates can wrap.
critique.cause: The 160px title and 270px URL columns together place the audit columns beyond the viewport. The 105px date column leaves only 84px for text.

critique.good: The beginning of the date column is visible on first sight, so readers get an earlier cue that the table contains audit results. The smaller overflow reduces the horizontal scroll distance.
critique.problems: URLs break into many fragments and dominate the row heights. At least one title word and several dates split, making rows hard to scan and compare. The status column still requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 155px URL column leaves only 134px for text, and the 120px title column leaves 99px, just short of the longest unbreakable title word. The date column leaves only 84px.

critique.good: The page titles have a comfortable measure and wrap mostly into coherent phrases. Rows remain reasonably compact, while the date column has enough width for intact values.
critique.problems: Some URL segments split inside words, making addresses harder to trace. The initial viewport shows the title and only part of each URL; both audit-result columns require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 270px URL column leaves 249px for text, less than the longest unbreakable segment. The 160px title and 270px URL columns already exceed the viewport together. The 68px status column also wraps its header.

critique.good: URLs avoid mid-word splits, and the rows are the most compact of the three designs. The 150px title column retains a readable hierarchy, and the date and status values have room to remain intact.
critique.problems: The wide URL column puts the audit results furthest away from the page titles, increasing the distance a reader must scroll to compare results. Much of each URL also lies outside the initial viewport.
critique.cause: The 345px URL column provides 324px of text width, enough for the longest unbreakable segment, but pushes the date column to 495px from the table's left edge. The 68px status column wraps its header.

critique.good: The narrower table reduces horizontal scrolling and brings the beginning of the date column into the initial viewport. Dates and status values retain the same protected widths as in the other designs.
critique.problems: URLs fragment heavily, including breaks inside domains and path words, and tall rows make comparison slower. Some page titles also become choppy. Only a sliver of the dates is visible initially, so their presence at the viewport edge offers little practical benefit.
critique.cause: The 200px URL column leaves only 179px for text, producing nine mid-word splits and cells up to six lines tall. The 130px title column also forces more wrapping.

r0A.idea: Fit the viewport, preserving room for dates and status codes while accepting substantial title and URL splitting.

r0B.idea: Use moderate horizontal scrolling to give titles and URLs more breathing room while keeping dates and status codes intact.

r0C.idea: Favor legibility with enough space for the longest uninterrupted URL segment and single-line audit headers, at the cost of substantial scrolling.

r1A.idea: Refine r0B with more URL space and enough date width to keep dates intact. Keep the status header wrapped to reduce the distance needed to reach the results.

r1B.idea: Give titles and URLs more room while retaining compact result columns. Test whether fewer awkward URL breaks justify the extra horizontal scrolling.

r1C.idea: Try a narrower scrolling compromise: keep dates and status codes intact, expose the start of the date column initially, and reduce the distance to the audit results while accepting more URL wrapping.

r2A.idea: Refine r1B by giving dates the full 96px of text space they need. Keep the successful title and URL proportions and the compact status column.

r2B.idea: Give the URL its full 324px longest-word allowance to reduce forced splits, while retaining readable title wrapping and intact dates. This tests whether cleaner URLs justify more horizontal scrolling.

r2C.idea: Test a middle ground between r1A and r1C: keep the URL wider than in r1C, allow 109px for title text, and reserve enough space for dates. More of the audit area comes into view at the cost of taller rows.

r3A.idea: Combine r2A's more comfortable title width with r2B's split-free URL width. This favors intact identifiers and compact rows while retaining the existing date and status widths.

r3B.idea: Reduce the URL width by 45px from r2B to bring audit results closer while keeping a readable title column. Check whether the resulting splits are limited enough to justify the shorter horizontal scroll.

r3C.idea: Fit the title and URL columns together within 359px so the initial viewport shows both destination fields. This accepts more wrapping and likely URL splits in exchange for a complete first view of the identifying columns.

understanding.purpose: Audit page links and their latest check results for Q1 2025.
understanding.reading: Readers identify a page by its title, inspect its URL, then compare the last-checked date and status code across rows. Each row should remain easy to follow across the table.
groups: Page title and URL identify the destination together.
Last checked and status code describe the audit result and support comparison across pages.
keep_intact: Status codes and dates should remain intact where possible.
URL components and page-title words should remain intact where space permits.
may_wrap: Page titles can wrap naturally between words.
URLs can wrap at meaningful separators; long uninterrupted segments may need splitting in narrower designs.
Headers can wrap when the corresponding data remains readable.

bad.why: The narrow title and URL columns split words and identifiers repeatedly, producing very tall rows that are difficult to scan.
URLs break inside words and leave awkward fragments, including isolated hyphens; the resulting tall rows weaken the connection between each title and its audit data.
Several URL components split mid-word, including a lone final letter, and the narrow title column adds frequent wrapping without bringing the audit columns meaningfully into view.

final.rationale: r2B gives page titles enough room to remain recognizable while allowing URL components to wrap without mid-word splits. The date fits on one line, and the compact status column preserves space for the longer fields. The cost is substantial horizontal scrolling: the initial viewport shows the titles and only part of the URLs, while the audit results lie to the right.

general: Give identifiers enough width to preserve meaningful character sequences when readers must inspect or compare them.
Judge horizontal scrolling alongside wrapping and row height; reducing overflow can make individual records harder to read.
Size columns according to their content and role rather than making them equal.
specific: The URL column needs about 345px including padding to accommodate this inventory's longest unbreakable component.
A 117px date column keeps the Last checked header on one line, while the status column can remain comparatively narrow.

final.tradeoffs: r3B reduces scrolling by 45px relative to r2B and keeps the same table height, but introduces two mid-word splits. r3A gives titles slightly more room at the cost of another 10px of scrolling.
final.uncertain: Designers may value seeing more of each URL on the first screen or reaching the audit results sooner over preserving every URL component. The ranges are conservative estimates around r2B, not browser-verified equivalence intervals; changes near wrapping thresholds can alter individual rows.

A.why: Titles remain readable and URLs wrap into manageable blocks, giving rows a useful rhythm. The date and status columns require horizontal scrolling, and much of each URL lies beyond the initial viewport.

B.why: Titles scan well, but URLs wrap across several lines and extend beyond the viewport. Dates and status codes are also off-screen, so auditing a row requires scrolling.

C.why: The visible layout resembles B: titles are readable, but long URL blocks extend beyond the viewport and the audit fields require scrolling.

D.why: More of the date column is initially visible, but URLs break repeatedly inside words and become difficult to follow. Some dates and title words also split, while status remains off-screen.

E.why: The wider URL column reduces URL wrapping, but the narrow title column creates tall, uneven title blocks and splits some words. The wider table also puts the audit fields farther off-screen.

F.why: All four columns fit in the viewport, but titles, URLs and dates break into fragments. Very tall rows make it difficult to scan and compare the audit results.

reviews.unsure: The supplied images show only the left portion of the wider layouts, so the full widths of their URL, date and status columns and the total scrolling distance cannot be judged directly. B and C appear identical in the visible area.

A.why: Page titles remain readable and rows have a manageable rhythm, though URLs continue beyond the viewport and the audit columns require horizontal scrolling.

B.why: The narrow title column creates frequent wrapping and taller rows, while much of the URL and the audit columns still require scrolling.

C.why: Titles wrap mostly at word boundaries and rows remain compact; URLs and the audit columns still extend beyond the initial viewport.

D.why: The URL column breaks addresses into many short fragments, making rows tall. Dates are partly split or beyond the viewport, and status codes require scrolling.

E.why: All columns fit initially, but titles and URLs break within words throughout, dates split, and very tall rows make comparison difficult.

F.why: Readable title wrapping and moderate row heights support scanning, although URLs and the audit columns require horizontal scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The supplied images cut off the right side of A, B, C, D and F, so I cannot judge the full URL widths, the date and status columns, or the total scrolling distance. A and F appear identical in the visible area.
